analysis.one_liner: Forces federal agencies to prove a rule's benefits justify its costs before issuing health, safety, and environmental protections, and lets Congress veto major rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee approved the bill in May 1995 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the bill never received a Senate vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every federal agency to attach a detailed cost-benefit analysis to any 'major rule' — one costing the economy $100 million or more — and to prepare formal risk assessments for rules touching health, safety, or the environment. The President or the budget director could designate a rule as major, and that designation could not be challenged in court. The Senate committee version also let Congress vote down major rules after agencies issued them. The rules at stake are the kind issued by the EPA, OSHA, FDA, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, and other agencies that limit pollution, workplace hazards, unsafe drugs, and dangerous products.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing expensive new regulations gain if the bill passes. The added analysis, review, and possible congressional veto would make each major rule slower and harder to issue, and would give regulated industries more opportunities to challenge or block rules before they take effect. Companies could also argue in court that a rule's costs outweigh its benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies to issue a preliminary and final cost-benefit analysis for every major rule, and to show that the benefits justify the costs and that no cheaper alternative would achieve equivalent risk reduction.
Lets the President or the OMB Director designate rules as major and review agencies' analyses, with those executive determinations explicitly exempted from judicial review.
Sets up a procedure for Congress to disapprove major rules after they are issued, including congressional veto and presidential override provisions.
Requires market-based mechanisms to be assessed for major rules, especially environmental ones, which supporters said would achieve the same goals at lower cost.
Limits judicial review of agency compliance with the new analysis requirements, reducing the ability of outside parties to challenge the process itself.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passes, the cost falls on people who rely on federal protections — workers covered by safety rules, consumers protected from unsafe products, and communities affected by pollution — because each major rule would take longer to issue and would be easier to block. Agencies would also spend staff time on paperwork instead of enforcement and rule-writing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities exposed to hazards

drawbacks.text: The requirements would delay or stop major health, safety, and environmental rules; every covered agency listed in the bill — the EPA, Department of Labor, FDA, CPSC, Transportation, Energy, Agriculture, Interior, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission — is one whose main job is protecting the public.

The President's or OMB Director's decision about which rules count as major, and how agencies' analyses are reviewed, could not be challenged in court, concentrating power over public protections in the executive branch without judicial checks.

The committee-added congressional veto would let a minority of legislators block a finalized rule through a procedural vote, adding another point where public protections can be stopped after years of work.

Cost-benefit analysis is genuinely hard for protective rules: benefits like avoided cancers or saved lives are difficult to monetize, so a legal requirement to show benefits 'justify' costs tends to weigh against precautionary rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — smarter, less costly regulation — has real merit, and some provisions (better risk communication, peer review, market-based alternatives, periodic review of old rules) could improve rule quality on the merits. But the design is not neutral: the hardest-hit agencies are the ones protecting workers, consumers, and the environment, the new executive reviews and the congressional veto create multiple choke points where a rule can be stopped, and the judicial-review carve-outs shield those choke points from challenge. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill's practical effect would be fewer and slower protections, with the heaviest burdens falling on rules with large, diffuse public benefits and concentrated private costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's calendar of pending business in May 1995, but the Senate leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and the Congress ended in January 1997 with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator William Roth introduced the Regulatory Reform Act of 1995 in the Senate on January 27, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs.
On March 23, 1995, the Committee on Governmental Affairs ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute — a rewritten version of the bill.
On May 25, 1995, the committee reported the bill with a substitute amendment as Senate Report 104-88, and members filed additional views signaling dissent within the committee.
The reported version added congressional veto and presidential override procedures for major rules, expanding the bill beyond cost-benefit analysis.
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 117 — the waiting list for bills awaiting floor action.
No further action followed: the bill never received a Senate floor vote, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on federal health, safety, and environmental protections are better off, because the bill never passed and the EPA, OSHA, FDA, and other agencies' rulemaking was not saddled with the new veto points. Regulated industries, which had sought the procedural hurdles, gained nothing from the bill's death but also lost nothing.

for.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
for.role: Senator from Delaware; sponsor and committee chair who reported the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as its sponsor, reported it out of the Governmental Affairs Committee with a substitute amendment.

for.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over federal regulatory procedure
for.what_they_did: Held a markup and reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on March 23, 1995.

for.name: 104th Congress Republican majority
for.role: Senate and House majorities elected in 1994 running on a regulatory-reform agenda
for.what_they_did: Made regulatory reform, including cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment mandates, a centerpiece of the 1995 legislative agenda alongside companion House legislation.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the Legislative Calendar on May 25, 1995.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed the congressional regulatory-reform bills of 1995, whose cost-benefit mandates, risk-assessment requirements, and congressional review provisions were widely described as capable of delaying or blocking major public-health and environmental rules.

against.name: Consumer, labor, and environmental organizations
against.role: Public-interest groups focused on health, safety, and environmental protections
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the 1995 regulatory reform bills, arguing the new analysis and review requirements would stall worker-safety, consumer, and environmental rules.

against.name: Committee members filing additional views
against.role: Members of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed additional views with the committee report, registering formal disagreement with the bill as reported.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred, so the record shows no party breakdown; the bill was sponsored and reported by a Senate Republican, the 1995 regulatory-reform push was a Republican priority, and committee members filed additional views in dissent, with the broader opposition coming from Democrats and public-interest groups.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and chemical, energy, and mining companies regulated by the EPA and Interior
industries.note: The bill would make every EPA major rule slower and easier to block through cost-benefit requirements, OMB review, congressional veto, and court challenges on the grounds that costs outweigh benefits. The public bears that cost in dirtier air and water and slower cleanup of hazards.

industries.industry: Employers subject to Labor Department (OSHA) workplace-safety rules
industries.note: OSHA is a covered agency, so workplace-safety rules would face the new analysis, review, and veto requirements, delaying protections that reduce worker injuries and deaths.

industries.industry: Drug, food, and consumer-product manufacturers regulated by the FDA and CPSC
industries.note: FDA and CPSC are covered agencies; product-safety and food and drug rules would take longer to issue and would be more vulnerable to challenge, while the bill carves out from review the rules that approve products for market.

industries.industry: Transportation and nuclear sectors (DOT, DOE, NRC rules)
industries.note: These agencies' safety rules would face the same new procedural hurdles, slowing rulemaking on hazards like transport of dangerous goods and reactor safety.
